lessons.title: Reader and Writer contracts
lessons.summary: If the source text becomes "go", what prints?
explanation:
io.Reader fills a supplied byte slice and returns a byte count plus an error. A reader may return data and an error together, so process n bytes before deciding what the error means. io.Writer must report how much it accepted; a short write requires an error.

Here Read receives a two-byte destination slice and returns how many bytes it filled plus an error. Write receives only those n bytes and returns how many it accepted plus an error. The explicit calls use an in-memory strings.Reader and bytes.Buffer; process returned bytes before interpreting a possible read error. The printed nil comparisons describe this particular successful read/write, not a promise that every Reader behaves identically.
```go
package main
import ("fmt"; "strings"; "bytes")
func main() {
    src := strings.NewReader("go")
    buf := make([]byte, 2)
    n, readErr := src.Read(buf)
    var dst bytes.Buffer
    written, writeErr := dst.Write(buf[:n])
    fmt.Println(n, readErr == nil)
    fmt.Println(written, writeErr == nil, dst.String())
}
```
Expected output: 2 true; 2 true go.

io.Copy transfers until EOF or another failure and returns the total bytes written plus an error. strings.NewReader supplies text bytes and bytes.Buffer collects them, so this example uses no files or network. Normal source exhaustion is not returned as an io.Copy error.

lessons.title: Atomic counters
lessons.summary: If each update adds 2 instead of 1, what prints?
explanation: atomic.Int64 provides Add and Load operations on an integer. Its zero value starts at zero, and Add returns the new value. Do not copy an atomic object after first use. Atomic operations have sequentially consistent ordering, not a promise about a particular implementation speed.

Two workers update the same typed atomic and finish before Load. This avoids lost increments for the one counter. Combining several separate Load and Store calls would not automatically make an entire algorithm atomic or preserve an invariant involving other fields.

Store replaces one atomic integer with its supplied value; Load returns its current value. This sequential companion has no goroutines and is not a read-modify-write operation. Separate Load and Store calls would still not make an increment atomic.

```go
package main
import ("fmt"; "sync/atomic")
func main() {
    var count atomic.Int64
    count.Store(7)
    fmt.Println(count.Load())
    count.Store(2)
    fmt.Println(count.Load())
}
```

lessons.title: Cancellation-aware worker lifetime
lessons.summary: If cancellation happens before starting the goroutine instead, what prints after done?
explanation: Cancellation alone does not wait for a goroutine to exit. This owner supplies a context, cancels it and then waits for a separate done channel. The worker owns closing done using defer, so main returns only after cleanup and result assignment.

The worker receives from ctx.Done; if cancellation already happened, that receive is immediately ready. This handles both cancellation before start and cancellation while waiting without a timing assumption. A worker doing other blocking work would also need cancellation-aware operations at those boundaries.

Complete local Go example; the app itself does not execute it:
```go
package main

import (
"fmt"
"context"
)


func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
    defer cancel()
    done := make(chan struct{})
    result := "waiting"
    go func() {
        defer close(done)
        <-ctx.Done()
        result = "stopped"
    }()
    cancel()
    <-done
    fmt.Println(result)
}
```

lessons.title: HTTP client deadlines and transport
lessons.summary: If the context deadline is already in the past, what does this fake transaction report?
explanation:
http.Client delegates a single transaction to its RoundTripper. This fake transport returns an in-memory response and never calls the default transport, DNS, a listener or a socket. io.NopCloser wraps the strings.Reader with a Close method that does nothing; it does not acquire or release an external resource. request.Context() takes no arguments and returns the context attached to that request. Calling Err on that returned context observes whether cancellation or a deadline has already ended it; it does not create a new context.

NewRequestWithContext attaches the context; a one-hour timeout here is a bound, not a timing assertion. Defer cancel releases context resources. On successful Do, close the response body even when reading fails. A received HTTP error status is not automatically a Do transport error; inspect StatusCode separately. The fixture reads only its known tiny in-memory body.

io.ReadAll receives the response body as a Reader, consumes its remaining bytes and returns a byte slice plus an error. It can allocate for all remaining input, so this example deliberately supplies only its known tiny body.
